scope: Physics AS mock practicals 1-6 and Chemistry covered practicals 1,2,3,10 only; no buffers and no untaught Chemistry RP7-12 introduced
notes: Ten wholly original written, data-analysis questions. Mark point method and numerical evidence separately; automatic marks provisional and final teacher/student review remains available. Not official past papers or mark schemes. No unsupervised practical handling instructions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP1 stretched string: frequency, controls and uncertainty
questions.prompt: A stationary wave on a stretched string has vibrating length L = (0.750 ± 0.008) m, tension T = (18.0 ± 0.7) N and mass per unit length μ = (0.0080 ± 0.0002) kg m⁻¹. The fundamental frequency is f = (1/2L)√(T/μ). (a) Calculate f. (b) Predict f if the tension is quadrupled while L and μ stay fixed. (c) Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the original f by adding relevant maximum fractional uncertainties. (d) State the physical reason for keeping the mode number fixed when comparing frequencies. [7 marks]
markPoints: The fundamental frequency is f = 31.6 Hz (approximately).
Four times the tension doubles f because f is proportional to √T.
The new fundamental frequency is approximately 63.2 Hz.
Percentage length uncertainty = 0.008/0.750 × 100 = 1.07%.
Different harmonics have different frequencies; compare the same fundamental mode so observed changes follow the tested variable.
questions.modelAnswer: Substitute in f = (1/2×0.750)√(18.0/0.0080). The fundamental frequency is f = 31.6 Hz (approximately). Four times the tension doubles f because f is proportional to √T. The new fundamental frequency is approximately 63.2 Hz. Percentage length uncertainty = 0.008/0.750 × 100 = 1.07%. Percentage uncertainty in f ≈ 1.07 + ½(0.7/18.0 × 100) + ½(0.0002/0.0080 × 100) = 4.26%. Different harmonics have different frequencies; compare the same fundamental mode so observed changes follow the tested variable.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP2 double-slit: fringe interval and uncertainty
questions.prompt: In a Young double-slit data analysis, the distance across eight consecutive fringe intervals is (16.0 ± 0.5) mm. Slit separation a = (0.350 ± 0.010) mm and screen distance D = (1.40 ± 0.02) m. (a) Determine the mean fringe width w. (b) Use w = λD/a to calculate wavelength λ in metres and nanometres. (c) Estimate its maximum percentage uncertainty from the given readings. (d) Explain why several intervals were measured together. [7 marks]
markPoints: Eight intervals across 16.0 mm give w = 16.0/8 = 2.00 mm.
Convert w = 2.00 × 10⁻³ m and a = 3.50 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Rearrange λ = wa/D.
Percentage uncertainty from fringe span = 0.5/16.0 × 100 = 3.13%.
Maximum percentage uncertainty in λ ≈ 3.13 + (0.010/0.350×100) + (0.02/1.40×100) = 7.41%.
Measuring several fringe intervals together reduces the percentage reading uncertainty compared with measuring one tiny gap.
questions.modelAnswer: Eight intervals across 16.0 mm give w = 16.0/8 = 2.00 mm. Convert w = 2.00 × 10⁻³ m and a = 3.50 × 10⁻⁴ m. Rearrange λ = wa/D. λ = 2.00×10⁻³ × 3.50×10⁻⁴ / 1.40 = 5.00×10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm. Percentage uncertainty from fringe span = 0.5/16.0 × 100 = 3.13%. Maximum percentage uncertainty in λ ≈ 3.13 + (0.010/0.350×100) + (0.02/1.40×100) = 7.41%. Measuring several fringe intervals together reduces the percentage reading uncertainty compared with measuring one tiny gap.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP3 free fall: graph-based g and gradient uncertainty
questions.prompt: A graph of vertical distance fallen h (m) against t² (s²) gives a best-fit gradient 4.88 m s⁻². Steepest and shallowest acceptable gradients are 5.06 and 4.72 m s⁻². Assume the object starts from rest and air resistance is negligible. (a) Explain why gradient = g/2. (b) Calculate g. (c) Estimate the absolute uncertainty in g using the larger deviation from the best-fit gradient, and express it as a percentage. (d) State a reason the fitted line should not automatically be forced through the origin. [6 marks]
markPoints: From h = ½gt², on a plot of h versus t² the gradient equals g/2.
Calculated g = 2×4.88 = 9.76 m s⁻².
Largest gradient deviation = max(5.06−4.88, 4.88−4.72) = 0.18 m s⁻².
Absolute uncertainty in g is 2×0.18 = 0.36 m s⁻².
Percentage uncertainty = 0.36/9.76 × 100 ≈ 3.7%.
An observed non-zero intercept could indicate timing/height offsets; forcing zero can conceal a systematic error.
questions.modelAnswer: From h = ½gt², on a plot of h versus t² the gradient equals g/2. Calculated g = 2×4.88 = 9.76 m s⁻². Largest gradient deviation = max(5.06−4.88, 4.88−4.72) = 0.18 m s⁻². Absolute uncertainty in g is 2×0.18 = 0.36 m s⁻². Percentage uncertainty = 0.36/9.76 × 100 ≈ 3.7%. An observed non-zero intercept could indicate timing/height offsets; forcing zero can conceal a systematic error.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP4 Young modulus: wire area and squared-diameter uncertainty
questions.prompt: For a wire of original length (1.40 m), diameter (0.320 ± 0.010) mm, a force of 12.0 N produces extension (1.40 ± 0.05) mm within the proportional region. Assume the force and original length uncertainties are negligible. (a) Find its original cross-sectional area. (b) Determine stress, strain and Young modulus E. (c) Estimate the combined maximum percentage uncertainty in E due to diameter and extension. [7 marks]
markPoints: Convert diameter d = 3.20×10⁻⁴ m; A = πd²/4.
Cross-sectional area A = 8.04×10⁻⁸ m².
Tensile stress = F/A = 12.0/(8.04×10⁻⁸) ≈ 1.49×10⁸ Pa.
Tensile strain = extension/original length = (1.40×10⁻³)/1.40 = 1.00×10⁻³.
Young modulus E = stress/strain ≈ 1.49×10¹¹ Pa.
Diameter contributes 2×(0.010/0.320×100) = 6.25% to uncertainty in E because area depends on d².
Extension contributes (0.05/1.40×100) = 3.57%; combined maximum ≈ 9.82%.
questions.modelAnswer: Convert diameter d = 3.20×10⁻⁴ m; A = πd²/4. Cross-sectional area A = 8.04×10⁻⁸ m². Tensile stress = F/A = 12.0/(8.04×10⁻⁸) ≈ 1.49×10⁸ Pa. Tensile strain = extension/original length = (1.40×10⁻³)/1.40 = 1.00×10⁻³. Young modulus E = stress/strain ≈ 1.49×10¹¹ Pa. Diameter contributes 2×(0.010/0.320×100) = 6.25% to uncertainty in E because area depends on d². Extension contributes (0.05/1.40×100) = 3.57%; combined maximum ≈ 9.82%.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP5 resistivity: measured R–length gradient
questions.prompt: In an idealised resistance-versus-length data set, R = 1.40 Ω at L = 0.350 m and R = 2.80 Ω at L = 0.700 m, for a uniform wire of diameter 0.500 mm. (a) Determine the gradient of R versus L, including units. (b) Calculate the cross-sectional area. (c) Obtain resistivity ρ in Ω m. (d) Explain why taking the graph gradient is preferable to assuming every measured resistance has zero contact resistance. [6 marks]
markPoints: Diameter is 0.500 mm = 5.00×10⁻⁴ m.
Area A = πd²/4 = 1.96×10⁻⁷ m².
Use gradient R/L = ρ/A, so ρ = gradient × A.
A non-zero constant contact resistance shifts the intercept but does not change the R-versus-L gradient.
questions.modelAnswer: Graph gradient ΔR/ΔL = (2.80−1.40)/(0.700−0.350) = 4.00 Ω m⁻¹. Diameter is 0.500 mm = 5.00×10⁻⁴ m. Area A = πd²/4 = 1.96×10⁻⁷ m². Use gradient R/L = ρ/A, so ρ = gradient × A. Resistivity ρ = 4.00×1.9635×10⁻⁷ = 7.85×10⁻⁷ Ω m. A non-zero constant contact resistance shifts the intercept but does not change the R-versus-L gradient.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP6 terminal p.d. graph and load prediction
questions.prompt: Two points on an idealised straight line of terminal p.d. V (y-axis) against current I (x-axis) are (0.25 A, 1.42 V) and (0.75 A, 1.18 V). (a) Find the graph gradient and internal resistance r. (b) Determine the emf ε. (c) Predict terminal p.d. and lost volts at 1.00 A. (d) Explain why a negative slope is expected. [6 marks]
markPoints: Since V = ε−Ir, internal resistance r = +0.48 Ω.
Extrapolate to I = 0: ε = V+Ir = 1.42 + (0.25×0.48) = 1.54 V.
Lost volts at 1.00 A = Ir = 0.48 V.
Current flowing through the cell's internal resistance causes an increasing internal voltage drop, reducing terminal p.d.
questions.modelAnswer: Gradient ΔV/ΔI = (1.18−1.42)/(0.75−0.25) = −0.48 V A⁻¹. Since V = ε−Ir, internal resistance r = +0.48 Ω. Extrapolate to I = 0: ε = V+Ir = 1.42 + (0.25×0.48) = 1.54 V. Lost volts at 1.00 A = Ir = 0.48 V. Terminal p.d. at 1.00 A = 1.54−0.48 = 1.06 V. Current flowing through the cell's internal resistance causes an increasing internal voltage drop, reducing terminal p.d.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP1 titration: concordant titres and 2:1 stoichiometry
questions.prompt: An analysis of acid–base titration data uses a 25.0 cm³ sample of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ and NaOH of unknown concentration. Recorded NaOH titres are: rough 22.60 cm³; accurate 22.15, 22.20 and 22.25 cm³. Assume the three accurate titres are concordant to 0.10 cm³. The reaction is H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. (a) Determine the mean concordant titre. (b) Calculate the NaOH concentration to three significant figures. (c) Explain why the rough titre is not used in the mean. [7 marks]
markPoints: The three accurate titres 22.15, 22.20 and 22.25 cm³ agree within a 0.10 cm³ range.
Mean concordant titre = (22.15+22.20+22.25)/3 = 22.20 cm³.
From 1:2 stoichiometry, moles NaOH = 2×0.00250 = 0.00500 mol.
Convert the average NaOH volume to 0.02220 dm³.
Concentration NaOH = 0.00500/0.02220 = 0.225 mol dm⁻³ (3 s.f.).
The rough reading is an approximate preliminary estimate and is excluded from the concordant accurate mean.
questions.modelAnswer: The three accurate titres 22.15, 22.20 and 22.25 cm³ agree within a 0.10 cm³ range. Mean concordant titre = (22.15+22.20+22.25)/3 = 22.20 cm³. Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.100×25.0/1000 = 0.00250 mol. From 1:2 stoichiometry, moles NaOH = 2×0.00250 = 0.00500 mol. Convert the average NaOH volume to 0.02220 dm³. Concentration NaOH = 0.00500/0.02220 = 0.225 mol dm⁻³ (3 s.f.). The rough reading is an approximate preliminary estimate and is excluded from the concordant accurate mean.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP2 cooling correction: enthalpy and underestimation
questions.prompt: In a calorimetry data exercise the initial solution temperature is 19.5 °C. The recorded maximum is 31.9 °C, while extrapolation of the subsequent cooling trend gives a corrected maximum of 32.8 °C. The mass of solution is 40.0 g, specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and 0.0400 mol of reaction occurred. (a) Calculate corrected ΔT, heat gained by solution, and molar reaction enthalpy with sign. (b) Explain why using the recorded maximum rather than the corrected one would underestimate the magnitude of exothermic ΔH. [7 marks]
markPoints: Use the extrapolated maximum 32.8 °C to correct for cooling before the maximum reading.
Corrected temperature change ΔT = 32.8−19.5 = 13.3 K.
Heat gained by solution q_solution = mcΔT = 40.0×4.18×13.3 = 2223.76 J.
Convert to 2.22376 kJ of heat gained by solution.
For 0.0400 mol reaction, magnitude |ΔH| = 2.22376/0.0400 = 55.6 kJ mol⁻¹.
Reaction enthalpy is ΔH = −55.6 kJ mol⁻¹ because the solution gains heat from an exothermic reaction.
The uncorrected maximum would give a smaller ΔT, hence smaller |q| and a less negative calculated ΔH.
questions.modelAnswer: Use the extrapolated maximum 32.8 °C to correct for cooling before the maximum reading. Corrected temperature change ΔT = 32.8−19.5 = 13.3 K. Heat gained by solution q_solution = mcΔT = 40.0×4.18×13.3 = 2223.76 J. Convert to 2.22376 kJ of heat gained by solution. For 0.0400 mol reaction, magnitude |ΔH| = 2.22376/0.0400 = 55.6 kJ mol⁻¹. Reaction enthalpy is ΔH = −55.6 kJ mol⁻¹ because the solution gains heat from an exothermic reaction. The uncorrected maximum would give a smaller ΔT, hence smaller |q| and a less negative calculated ΔH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP3 rate: interpreting constant-endpoint times
questions.prompt: In a classroom reaction-rate data set, the same fixed visual endpoint is reached in 280 s at 20 °C, 170 s at 30 °C and 100 s at 40 °C. Assume that a fixed amount of reaction occurs at the endpoint at every temperature. (a) Calculate the relative rate 1/t at 20 °C and 40 °C, with units. (b) Determine the factor by which relative rate changes between these temperatures. (c) Explain why the reciprocal time is only proportional to rate under the fixed-endpoint assumption. (d) Name two other conditions that must remain unchanged for a fair temperature comparison. [6 marks]
markPoints: At 20 °C, relative rate = 1/280 = 0.00357 s⁻¹.
At 40 °C, relative rate = 1/100 = 0.0100 s⁻¹.
Reciprocal time represents comparable mean rates only when the fixed endpoint corresponds to the same reaction progress each time.
Initial reactant concentration must be kept the same for each temperature comparison.
Reactant amounts or total volumes must remain the same; otherwise the amount to react or concentrations can change.
questions.modelAnswer: At 20 °C, relative rate = 1/280 = 0.00357 s⁻¹. At 40 °C, relative rate = 1/100 = 0.0100 s⁻¹. Relative rate ratio (1/100)/(1/280) = 280/100 = 2.80. Reciprocal time represents comparable mean rates only when the fixed endpoint corresponds to the same reaction progress each time. Initial reactant concentration must be kept the same for each temperature comparison. Reactant amounts or total volumes must remain the same; otherwise the amount to react or concentrations can change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP10 product: percentage yield and purity evidence
questions.prompt: An ester preparation data question gives a theoretical maximum of 0.160 mol of ester (Mr = 116.0). The recovered liquid product has mass 7.80 g, with a measured boiling range of 75–81 °C. A reference boiling point for the pure ester at the same pressure is 77 °C. (a) Determine theoretical mass and percentage yield. (b) State one plausible reason for a yield below 100%. (c) Explain what the broad boiling range does and does not establish about product purity. [6 marks]
markPoints: Theoretical ester mass = 0.160 mol × 116.0 g mol⁻¹ = 18.56 g.
Percentage yield = actual mass/theoretical mass × 100.
Some material may be lost during transfer or separation, so collected yield can be below 100%.
A broad boiling range spanning 75–81 °C is evidence the recovered liquid may contain impurities or mixed components.
A boiling range close to the reference value does not by itself prove chemical identity or complete purity; other evidence is needed.
questions.modelAnswer: Theoretical ester mass = 0.160 mol × 116.0 g mol⁻¹ = 18.56 g. Percentage yield = actual mass/theoretical mass × 100. Yield = 7.80/18.56 × 100 ≈ 42.0%. Some material may be lost during transfer or separation, so collected yield can be below 100%. A broad boiling range spanning 75–81 °C is evidence the recovered liquid may contain impurities or mixed components. A boiling range close to the reference value does not by itself prove chemical identity or complete purity; other evidence is needed.
